case_study_futbol-talent-pro.intro: I designed the user experience and information architecture for the MVP of a mobile-first platform focused on sports scouting.
case_study_futbol-talent-pro.challenge: Design a scalable MVP connecting three distinct user profiles (players, scouts, and clubs) while maintaining intuitive navigation and low cognitive load. The core technical objective was to ensure all design decisions were 100% viable for agile code implementation.
case_study_futbol-talent-pro.decision_1_body: Instead of exposing all features at once, I structured progressive access flows. This differentiated basic access from advanced features through a clear visual hierarchy.
case_study_futbol-talent-pro.decision_2_title: Progressive search to reduce cognitive load
case_study_futbol-talent-pro.decision_2_body: I proposed a simple, intuitive default search (name, position, region), encapsulating complex options under 'Advanced Filters' for power users.
case_study_futbol-talent-pro.decision_3_title: Gamification supported by a Design System
case_study_futbol-talent-pro.decision_3_body: To prevent cluttering the screen with rankings and badges, I built an atomic design system from scratch (tokens, consistent iconography, light/dark). This kept the interface clean.
case_study_futbol-talent-pro.delivered_1: Key interface designs for 3 user profiles
case_study_futbol-talent-pro.delivered_2: Complete atomic Design System (tokens, components, light/dark)
case_study_futbol-talent-pro.delivered_3: Lo-fi wireframes and user flows (anonymized version)
case_study_futbol-talent-pro.closing: I worked in parallel with the frontend developer, validating the technical feasibility of each screen. Operating under strict confidentiality rules required me to be extremely methodical: rigorously documenting the 'why' behind each UX decision and ensuring a seamless handoff.

case_study_el-ritual-del-tono.intro: I built a reverse search engine for guitarists: you search by artist and song, and the app returns the full signal chain (guitar, pedals, amplifier) to replicate that exact sound. MERN stack, deployed on Vercel.
case_study_el-ritual-del-tono.challenge: Letting a user add 5–8 products to the cart with a single click, without duplicating items, respecting stock, and syncing state between backend and Context API. The transaction had to feel atomic from the UI.
case_study_el-ritual-del-tono.decision_1_body: A dedicated endpoint that receives an array of IDs, validates availability in MongoDB, and returns only the addable items. The frontend updates the cart in a single operation, with no partially loaded products visible to the user.
case_study_el-ritual-del-tono.decision_2_body: David Gilmour and John Mayer use similar pedals. Modeling each gear as unique per artist would have blown up the database. Solution: an independent Gears collection where each Song points to reusable ObjectIds.
case_study_el-ritual-del-tono.decision_3_body: Instead of 50 artists × 10 tones, I focused on 13 iconic artists with 2 tones each. Simulated checkout in MongoDB instead of integrating Stripe. Enough to demonstrate the transactional flow without getting stuck on payment integrations.
case_study_el-ritual-del-tono.delivered_1: Node.js + Express backend with REST API and 3 MongoDB collections
case_study_el-ritual-del-tono.delivered_2: Next.js frontend + React Context API + Tailwind CSS
case_study_el-ritual-del-tono.delivered_3: Deployed on Vercel with end-to-end live demo (artist → song → cart → checkout)
case_study_el-ritual-del-tono.closing: Modeling data in MongoDB is fundamentally different from SQL. I chose subdocuments (Songs inside Artists) because 90% of queries are 'give me the songs by this artist': no populate needed, faster responses. If I were to redo it: authentication + user-shared setups to turn personal curation into a guitarist social network.

case_study_cabify-music-match.intro: Cabify already had a music option, but it only changed the radio station (dead tech). I designed Music Match: a feature that merges driver and passenger tastes via Spotify, without adding friction to the trip request flow.
case_study_cabify-music-match.challenge: Aligning the musical tastes of two people who just met, without either feeling they lost control. Prioritize the passenger, the driver gets uncomfortable; flip it, same problem. The solution couldn't be a unilateral override.
case_study_cabify-music-match.decision_1_body: Detects matches in genres and artists between both Spotify profiles and generates a temporary trip playlist. If there aren't enough matches, it offers pre-curated mood playlists (energizing, relaxing, neutral). And there's always 'Silence', because not everyone wants music.
case_study_cabify-music-match.decision_2_body: Linking Spotify can't add friction to the trip request flow. Skippable explanatory modal the first time. If skipped, Music Match doesn't appear. If linked, the feature activates automatically with a simple toggle to opt out.
case_study_cabify-music-match.decision_3_title: Validating the silence mode was key
case_study_cabify-music-match.decision_3_body: Research showed many people would rather hear nothing. Validating this avoided forcing a feature where sometimes the best solution is not using it. 'Silence' sits at the same hierarchical level as the other two options, not hidden in a menu.
case_study_cabify-music-match.delivered_1: iPhone 14 Figma prototype with onboarding, simulated OAuth, controls and settings
case_study_cabify-music-match.delivered_2: User flows tested with real drivers and passengers
case_study_cabify-music-match.delivered_3: UI aligned with Cabify's official brand guidelines (brand.cabify.com)
case_study_cabify-music-match.closing: The best features aren't the most complex. They're the ones that solve emotional problems (the discomfort of silence with a stranger) with simple tech (connecting two Spotify accounts). If I were to redo it: post-trip feedback to iterate the merge algorithm with real data and turn Music Match into a real competitive edge.

case_study_multibrand-design-system.intro: At No Country, a team of 6 across 3 countries, 5 weeks, we designed a multibrand Design System that lets multiple EdTech products share a common base without losing identity: 70% mandatory core, 30% customizable.
case_study_multibrand-design-system.challenge: Defining what belonged in the 70% core (immutable) vs the 30% customizable. Each brand wanted creative freedom, but too much customization breaks the educational consistency the system had to guarantee.
case_study_multibrand-design-system.decision_1_body: Before defining the system, we analyzed 4 real EdTech platforms (Coursera, edX, Udemy, Platzi) to identify common patterns. The personas weren't students, they were the designers and devs who would use the system.
case_study_multibrand-design-system.decision_2_title: Core as a brand invariant, not a visual style
case_study_multibrand-design-system.decision_2_body: The 70% core covers grid, spacing, radii, shadows, component behavior, AA accessibility, and UX patterns (onboarding, errors, progress). What's customizable: only primary/secondary/accent color, typography (3 pre-approved options), and iconography.
case_study_multibrand-design-system.decision_3_title: UX Writing as a system, not decoration
case_study_multibrand-design-system.decision_3_body: Voice and tone codified with full guidelines: clear, human, motivating without being over the top. Standardized microcopy ('Loading…', 'Saved'), empathetic error messages, and a brand adaptation system that adjusts tone without changing the fundamental voice.
case_study_multibrand-design-system.delivered_1: Tokens (color, typography, spacing, radii, shadows, motion) in Figma Variables with light/dark
case_study_multibrand-design-system.delivered_2: UI library: buttons, inputs, cards, navigation, modals, alerts, tables, progress bars
case_study_multibrand-design-system.delivered_3: Governance system + Notion documentation for non-technical teams
case_study_multibrand-design-system.closing: Designing a Design System is 30% visual design and 70% governance and documentation. Beautiful components are useless if nobody knows when to use them. Multicultural collaboration taught me to justify every decision: you can't just say 'I like it better this way'. If I were to redo it: fewer components, better documented.

case_study_recuerdalo.intro: I designed Recuérdalo: a reminder app for adults 70+ grounded in real research with users in the target age range, not on assumptions about what they 'need'. University project in inclusive UX.
case_study_recuerdalo.challenge: Balancing autonomy vs help. Older adults want to feel capable (the pride of overcoming challenges is huge) but they also need support when they get stuck. Too much help feels condescending. Too little drives abandonment.
case_study_recuerdalo.decision_1_title: Visible reversible steps, not blind flows
case_study_recuerdalo.decision_1_body: The key insight came from an 80-year-old interviewee: 'I start fine, but if I make a mistake in the third step, I don't know how to go back'. The solution wasn't to simplify, it was to make reversibility obvious. Numeric indicator (Step 1 of 3), large 'Back' buttons on every screen, immediate visual confirmations.
case_study_recuerdalo.decision_2_title: Architecture by emotional context, not by function
case_study_recuerdalo.decision_2_body: Open card sorting with 3 older users and 15 cards. They grouped by emotional context, not by type of function: 'My Obligations and Health', 'My People', 'To Entertain and Think', 'Important Things and Help'. The architecture followed that mapping, not a designer's logic.
case_study_recuerdalo.decision_3_title: Accessibility as foundation, not extra layer
case_study_recuerdalo.decision_3_body: Minimum 18px typography (vs the standard 14px) for aging vision. AA contrast across the board. 60×60px touch targets (vs the general 44px recommendation) for less precise fingers. Floating 'Help' button always visible: contextual tutorials or emergency contact call.
case_study_recuerdalo.delivered_1: Documented research: interviews, transcripts, affinity diagrams, the main user's journey map
case_study_recuerdalo.delivered_2: User personas with real quotes from interviewees
case_study_recuerdalo.delivered_3: High-fidelity Figma prototype with every main screen
case_study_recuerdalo.closing: Inclusive design isn't an aesthetic layer you add at the end, it's the foundation of a good experience. Designing for the 3 interviewees, with their visual limitations and fragile sequential memory, ended up creating a product that's clearer and more robust for everyone. If I were to redo it: a 'Family Peace-of-Mind System' that links the app with the user's children to reduce family anxiety and strengthen the support network.

about.title: ABOUT GOTYA
about.body_1: Designing for humans means stepping out of the “design mood”. It means sitting at any table and understanding the dynamics of every department to deliver real value.
about.body_2: Gotya comes from gotcha (“I get it”). It’s the confirmation that the core idea is captured. That understanding is what turns a business goal into an experience people remember.

case_study_paseo-guemes-hotel.intro: Paseo Güemes Hotel is a 3-star hotel in the heart of Salta City, in the bar district and steps away from the historic center. It opened in February 2026, so I joined a brand new business still defining its audience across domestic tourism, international travelers, and a corporate segment.
case_study_paseo-guemes-hotel.challenge: Digitally, the starting point was minimal: domain, hosting, and WordPress installed, and the booking engine already running, but no site built. Without its own website, the hotel depended on OTAs and their commissions, lost direct bookings, and received scattered inquiries in messages that got lost without context. The constraints shaped the path: a tight budget, a site the hotel itself could maintain, inherited hosting and domain, content arriving in pieces, and a booking engine I had no direct access to, since the manager administers it.
case_study_paseo-guemes-hotel.process: I did not go straight to building pages. I started with a brief for the owner (business, goals, competitors, and audience), ran an analysis of the Salta hotel market with a positioning map and a definition of the ideal guest, and only then built desktop and mobile wireframes in Figma.
case_study_paseo-guemes-hotel.decision_1_title: Direct booking first, OTAs in the background
case_study_paseo-guemes-hotel.decision_1_body: The whole site pushes toward the hotel own booking engine, with OTAs left as a discovery window rather than the main channel. The business goal was to cut commissions and stop losing direct bookings, so the messaging and the CTAs were organized around that.
case_study_paseo-guemes-hotel.decision_2_title: A stack the client can edit, not custom development
case_study_paseo-guemes-hotel.decision_2_body: With a tight budget and the need for the hotel to maintain the site without depending on me, an editable stack beat a hand-built development. I picked a lightweight theme with a header and footer builder included, to protect mobile performance without adding licenses.
case_study_paseo-guemes-hotel.decision_3_title: Hero hierarchy and CTAs spread across the journey
case_study_paseo-guemes-hotel.decision_3_body: A hero with video of the Güemes Monument, because location is the hotel number one asset, and a single strong booking CTA. Secondary calls to action were spread across sections so the booking button would not lose its impact by repeating in every block. For inquiries I added a floating WhatsApp button instead of relying on Instagram messages: it arrives with context and does not get lost.
case_study_paseo-guemes-hotel.delivered_1: Mobile-first site with Home, Rooms, Benefits, Location, and Contact
case_study_paseo-guemes-hotel.delivered_2: Identity applied end to end: palette extracted from the logo, type system, and logo versions for light and dark backgrounds
case_study_paseo-guemes-hotel.delivered_3: Direct booking integrated, WhatsApp and forms, plus local SEO foundations, automated backups, and optimized performance
case_study_paseo-guemes-hotel.closing: The site is about to go live, so there are no hard metrics yet and I would rather not invent them. What is observable is already clear: the hotel moves from depending on OTAs to having its own direct booking channel, gains a digital presence that did not exist before, and inquiries now arrive through WhatsApp with context instead of getting lost. Building with content that arrived in pieces forced me to work in blocks and leave temporary placeholders instead of stalling. I also learned to choose the robust flow over the flashy one: not forcing the booking engine inside the hero and solving it with a direct button instead. If I did it again, I would lock down the real photos earlier, since they are the asset that converts most, and request the booking engine credentials from day one.

case_study_pulso-creativo.intro: Pulso Creativo is a B2B consultancy with over 25 years of experience in marketing, branding, and coaching. They needed an institutional platform that worked as a digital calling card and reflected their level of corporate expertise to decision makers.
case_study_pulso-creativo.challenge: Without a digital channel of their own, they kept losing chances to show authority: there was no centralized space to display major clients, and no flow prepared to receive business inquiries with enough context to qualify B2B leads. Two concrete constraints came on top: native WordPress templates clashed with the visual builder layout (misaligned legal pages, issues with the transparent header), and the client delivered a very dense volume of copy for the success stories that threatened readability on mobile.
case_study_pulso-creativo.process: The build started from a block-based layout, prioritizing carousels and grids. On top of that I worked iteratively on the interface and the copywriting, turning long paragraphs into scannable formats and adjusting layout behavior to guarantee a fluid responsive experience.
case_study_pulso-creativo.decision_1_body: Instead of relying only on a static form, I set up a dynamic CTA that captures the page the visitor is looking at. That way the consultants know exactly which service the prospect was browsing before writing, commercial context that is worth its weight in gold when closing.
case_study_pulso-creativo.decision_2_title: Success stories as bullets, not walls of text
case_study_pulso-creativo.decision_2_body: I dropped the continuous copy the client sent and turned it into an icon list. The corporate user does not read, they scan: this lowers cognitive load, improves line length on desktop, avoids infinite scroll on mobile, and puts the hard results in plain sight.
case_study_pulso-creativo.decision_3_title: Corporate contrast and a limited reading width
case_study_pulso-creativo.decision_3_body: A dark footer and solid backgrounds in the more bureaucratic sections, with text capped at 800px wide. It avoids the visual fatigue of edge-to-edge lines, clearly separates information hierarchies, and gives the site a premium visual close.
case_study_pulso-creativo.delivered_1: Full-width responsive site with a dual contact system: form and WhatsApp
case_study_pulso-creativo.delivered_2: UX rewrite of the content delivered by the client, from dense copy to a scannable format
case_study_pulso-creativo.delivered_3: Server-side performance optimization and production launch with organic indexing in Google Search Console
case_study_pulso-creativo.closing: The business now projects authority from the first scroll, and the contact funnel is optimized: inquiries come in qualified and direct. The client logo carousel, with native touch behavior, validates the consultancy track record within the first seconds of browsing. The biggest lesson was UX negotiation with the client: mediating between the business need to tell every bit of its operational effort and the end user need to consume fast, concise information.
